first_impression.reaction: Two paragraphs about how the guide was written before I get anything, which is a bit much on the train. But the Key Takeaways are right under it and the table straight after is exactly what I searched for. Stayed for that.

journey.quote: This guide does it differently. Each custom is grouped by when it happens, from the week before to the morning after, and each meaning comes from a German heritage body, a German government page or a named editorial source.
journey.reaction: Okay, nice that it's sourced, but I wanted the traditions, not a description of the method. I skimmed past this.

journey.quote: The Polterabend is a noisy pre-wedding party where guests smash porcelain, never glass, and the couple sweep up the shards together.
journey.reaction: That's the kind of quick, specific answer I came for. Takeaways are short and readable on my phone.

journey.quote: In Germany, only the declaration before the registrar at the Standesamt creates a legal marriage, so the civil ceremony comes first.
journey.reaction: First bullet is about legal stuff. I searched for traditions, so I'd rather the first point was a custom. Not a big deal.

journey.section: German wedding traditions at a glance
journey.quote: | After the ceremony | Baumstamm saegen | The couple saw through a log together |
journey.reaction: The table is the best bit. In one screen I have the whole list in order. This is the part I'd screenshot. The spelling 'saegen' looks a bit off though, like a typo for the German word.

journey.quote: Its age is often told as pre-Christian, but even the Bavarian heritage wiki that mentions this only says "probably" and offers no evidence.
journey.reaction: I like that they admit when a story isn't proven. Feels more honest than the usual listicle.

journey.section: What an Australian couple should check
journey.quote: As at November 2026, the City of Hannover's official service page says foreign nationals marrying in Germany must in principle present a certificate of no impediment to marriage (Ehefaehigkeitszeugnis) from their home country.
journey.reaction: This whole stretch is long and written for Australians. I'm not Australian and not getting married in Germany, so I scrolled fast. Good that it's dated though.

journey.quote: The right hand, for both partners.
journey.reaction: Short, direct FAQ answers. This is what I want. I'd come back to this.

journey.quote: Follow the invitation and the couple's lead. Customs vary by region, so there is no single national dress code.
journey.reaction: If I was a guest Googling this, that answer doesn't really help me. Same with gifts: 'Ask the couple' isn't much.

unanswered_questions: As a guest, what is a normal gift or amount of money to give at a German wedding?
What should a guest actually wear, even roughly (suit, cocktail dress, traditional dress in Bavaria)?
Do I bring anything to a Polterabend if I'm invited, and do I bring my own porcelain?

turn_offs_found.quote: Most lists of German wedding traditions repeat the same handful of party games and the same origin stories, rarely with a source.
turn_offs_found.why: Opening on what other sites do wrong, rather than the answer. I have to get through two paragraphs before the takeaways.

turn_offs_found.quote: This is the part that matters most for an Australian couple.
turn_offs_found.why: A long legal and travel section in the middle of a traditions article. Not for me, and it pushes the reception customs (the fun bit) further down the page.
German words spelt without umlauts (saegen, Brautentfuehrung, Ehefaehigkeitszeugnis) look like errors to me and make me wonder about accuracy.

would_share_with: A friend going to a German wedding (the at-a-glance table)

cta_reaction.quote: If the paperwork is the part keeping you up at night, speak with a Wedded Advisor.
cta_reaction.why: I'm here for a quick answer, not planning a wedding in Germany. I might bookmark the site, but I wouldn't enquire today. The related link to wedding traditions in other countries is the one I might tap.

top_3_changes: Cut the intro to one or two sentences so the Key Takeaways and the at-a-glance table sit in the first screen, and lead the takeaways with a custom rather than the legal point.
Use proper German spelling with umlauts (Baumstamm sägen, Brautentführung) or explain the spelling once, as the transliterations read like typos.
Give guests something concrete in the dress and gift FAQs, or tighten the Australian legal section so the reception customs come sooner for casual readers.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Priya, a casual search visitor on her phone
No invented brand facts; missing info listed as unanswered questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments ignored
Missing business details and lack of prices not raised as must-fix, per orchestrator

open_questions.question: Is the umlaut-free spelling (saegen, Brautentfuehrung) a deliberate CMS or slug constraint? If not, a real reader sees it as a typo.

Low likelihood_to_enquire is expected for this persona (informational intent) and is not a defect in the draft.
